title: Congress discovers a spending limit. Immediately asks if it comes in a larger size.
My grandfather fixed the porch with three tools. The city commissioned a study to identify them.
Government efficiency tip Turn every three meetings into one canceled meeting.
My tax refund arrived. Always nice when your wallet writes you a thank-you note.
School board agenda: listen to parents. Moved to the end, after the workshop on listening.
The Constitution has seven articles. The instructions for my new dishwasher have twelve.
Government math The program is temporary. The department is eternal.
My neighbor and I solved the parking problem in ten minutes. We forgot to form a task force. Devastating oversight.
The farm-to-table movement discovered my grandfather. He called it bringing the tomatoes inside.
They promised a shovel-ready project. Turns out the shovel needed its own environmental review.
Small business Saturday The one day of the year the paperwork says it appreciates you.
My emergency fund has an emergency fund. We call that one Dad.
A federal agency announced a plan to reduce forms. Apply for a copy using Form 12-B.
My kid asked how a bill becomes law. I showed him the phone book and said, “Find the bill.”
Grandma’s free-market lesson Buy the cheap rake once. Buy the good rake after the cheap one breaks.
The town voted to ban leaf blowers. The first public hearing was canceled due to leaves.
Dad repaired the grill. The original manufacturer respectfully declined to believe him.
We need a national conversation about self-reliance. Dad started without us.
The permit office is paperless now. Please print your confirmation email and bring two copies.
Washington calls it a continuing resolution. Dad calls it refusing to decide what’s for dinner.
My uncle installed a clothesline. His electric dryer is now a seasonal employee.
We asked the state for a simpler licensing system. It sent us a flowchart with a legend.
Grandpa’s inflation calculator “What’d you pay for that?” followed by forty seconds of silence.

The campaign promised a government that fits in your pocket. Then it found the money in your other pocket.
Small-town public transit Wave at Bob. Bob has a truck.
The school board surveyed parents about survey fatigue. Please complete both pages.
The village put a QR code on the noticeboard. Grandma put the notice back.
The government launched a website to consolidate its websites. There are now two websites about consolidation.
My dad owns a level, a tape measure, and a pencil. Still somehow beats the app at hanging a shelf.
A century ago the town built a bridge. This year it finished the logo for the replacement.
Bureaucracy is an important part of composting. You need something to put underneath the leaves.
The town hired a consultant to recommend cuts. Excellent news. We found the first one.
Grandma’s economic outlook If the jar still has a lid, we are not buying containers.
I asked my congressman what a sunset clause was. He said we could discuss it at sunrise in ten years.
The local zoning board finally approved the lemonade stand. The children are now old enough to serve on the board.
I support a balanced budget. My bank has been very persuasive on the subject.
The town put a historic marker on the pothole. The repair is now subject to additional review.
Congress held a hearing on long lines. Seating was available by appointment only.
Dad’s infrastructure plan One trip to the hardware store, followed by three necessary amendments.
A regulatory agency asked for plain English. The request for it is eighty pages long.
Grandma called the town hall hotline. It was a gentleman named Earl. Everything was fixed by lunch.
The federal budget needed more transparency. So they released a PDF you can’t search.
The community garden elected a tomato chair. The zucchini immediately formed an opposition party.
I believe in limited government. Start by limiting the number of passwords required to pay it.
The county introduced a one-stop permit portal. It tells you which five offices to visit.
My neighbor said the barn needed a feasibility study. We looked up. It needed a roof.
The library still has the Constitution in large print. The budget requires a magnifying glass and a strong constitution.
The hardware store has a loyalty program. Grandpa has been loyal since 1978. Nobody asked for his phone number.
I brought a calculator to the budget hearing. Apparently, outside witnesses are prohibited.
My uncle mows the church lawn every Saturday. He calls it a riding ministry.
The city commissioned a report on unused office space. The report asked for a bigger office.
My youngest wants to be an entrepreneur. The lemonade stand has already charged me a convenience fee.
We refinanced the national debt. Even the calculator asked to speak to a human.
I told Dad a robot could mow the lawn. He said it could start by paying for the lawn.
There are two kinds of savings accounts. The kind you fund and the kind Congress refers to in speeches.
A sheep walked into the county fair. The judges said it had outstanding field experience.
My grandpa has never used a password manager. He has a coffee tin marked “mine.”
The grant application asked about community engagement. The volunteer fire chief wrote “We show up.”
The tax code includes a section on simplicity. I’d tell you the page number, but it has its own index.
Dad labels every coffee can of screws “misc.” It’s a decentralized inventory system.
The city hired a firm to improve the complaint line. Calls may now be ignored for quality assurance.
A town council votes to study transparency. The minutes will be released shortly after the sun burns out.
My aunt’s canning shelf is immaculate. Six quarts of peaches and zero quarterly earnings calls.
Every federal form wants my estimated income. I’d like their estimate of when this form will end.
The church potluck pioneered competition. Good luck keeping your job with store-bought pie.
A banker asked if I had any liquid assets. I showed him the coffee thermos Grandpa left me.
The county announced a program for backyard chickens. The chickens requested a copy of the pecking order.
My dad won the fiscal responsibility award. He saw the entry fee and declined.
The moving truck had to wait for a city permit. By the time it arrived, the kids had moved out.
I asked a farmer how he measures productivity. He pointed at a basket that wasn’t empty.
The town has a new sign that says “Preserve Rural Character.” It took down three old barns to make room for it.
Dad says you can learn economics at a flea market. Start by watching Mom walk away from a price tag.
My uncle brews his coffee strong. The spoon shifted the balance of power.
The city offered a workshop on cutting red tape. Scissors were provided pending approval.
A federal procurement officer walks into a hardware store. He leaves in six to eight fiscal quarters.
Grandma taught me the value of a dollar. She made me walk back to the driveway for one.

The taxpayer hotline promised a brief wait. I now qualify for an additional dependent.
The new municipal website is mobile-friendly. If you have a mobile printer.
Congress announced a bipartisan compromise. Both sides agreed to bill the third party.
My grandfather tracked his retirement in a notebook. When the market dropped he turned the page.
The school sent home a form asking how we teach initiative. My kid filled it out before I could object.
They say nothing in life is free. The church ladies said “Have another slice” and meant it.
The farm stand has an honor box. Imagine explaining that software to a procurement committee.
I fixed the porch light with a spare bulb. The city would call that an adaptive reuse initiative.
We formed a neighborhood watch. It mostly watches whether Hank put his flag up yet.
They made the rules for joining the rec league easier. Now the waiver comes with its own glossary.
My family keeps a biscuit starter older than most agencies. It has a better record of producing things.
The county needs three signatures for a picnic shelter. The ants moved in without permits.
A reporter asked Dad what he’d do with a windfall. He said, “Is the current roof still on?”
The city removed the stop sign to improve traffic flow. Residents installed a folding chair and brought it back by unanimous consent.
Grandma measures vanilla in her heart. She measures a grocery bill down to the penny.
The township asked for feedback on raising water rates. The neighbors sent a very detailed rain dance.
I keep my politics close to home. Our toughest election is who gets the last cinnamon roll.
The village has one traffic light and no traffic. The light still requested a staff increase.
Dad’s pension strategy is very complex. Every time he wants a new truck, he starts the old one.
The county streamlined public comments. You now get three minutes to summarize the seventy-page packet.
The kids turned the garage into a small business. Labor negotiations began when I charged them rent.
We bought a freezer to save money on meat. Grandpa bought the freezer used. He saved money on saving money.
The town rezoned a cornfield for economic vitality. The corn had been doing a decent job on its own.
My neighbor invests in tools. The dividends come back in casseroles.
A committee was formed to define “common sense.” It will reconvene after it agrees what “common” means.
Grandpa says politics is like fishing. The person who caught something doesn’t need to tell you how big it was.
The department rolled out a modern records system. The main feature is a picture of a filing cabinet.
Our family sporting event is competitive couponing. Mom is investigated annually for performance-enhancing circulars.
A local shop puts “Made Here” on the label. Dad still turns it over to check the fine print.
The federal budget is available in paperback. For lifting, bend your knees.
The town’s survey asked if we want lower taxes. The options were “strongly support” and “support with added services.”
My grandpa’s lawn mower has no software updates. It has an attitude and a string.
Washington streamlined the permitting process. The new flowchart folds into a smaller square.
The neighbors built a ramp in one weekend. They called the committee meeting a cookout.
I support local businesses. The hardware store knows my projects better than I do.
The library stocked a new book on government waste. Somebody reserved a conference room to discuss buying another copy.
Our county has a new Office of Collaboration. It works alongside the Office of Coordinating Collaboration.
I called Dad for help with a shelf. He came over with a stud finder and called it a family reunion.
I mentioned a kitchen remodel to Grandma. She moved the bread box and said, “How’s that?”
The local election was decided by eight votes. Thanksgiving dinner has never felt so mathematically fraught.
A city inspector was surprised by the beaver dam. Apparently the project had started before the comment period.
My family’s strategic grain reserve is in the pantry. It’s sponsored by Mom buying flour on sale.
The mayor promised an end to wasteful studies. A follow-up study will measure how it went.
Dad asked why I bought an extended warranty. Then showed me the chair he fixed with one screw.
Grandma’s dishwasher cycle has one setting. If you cooked, you dry.
The neighborhood newsletter introduced a fact-check column. It’s just Mrs. Grady calling your mother.
My father believes strongly in term limits. The lawn chair goes away at dusk.
The town asked for a five-year infrastructure plan. The road crew said, “Well, we were going to patch it Tuesday.”
I inherited the family tool chest. The part about returning borrowed sockets was legally binding.
Local control sounds complicated. Around here it means you know where the school board members buy groceries.
A small business owner walked into a forms office. He walked out with a thriving side business in binders.
I asked Dad whether he supports universal coverage. He handed me the other end of the tarp.
Grandma celebrated independence by making everything from scratch. She granted conditional independence to anyone who could roll dough.
The federal office adopted a “move fast” policy. Implementation is scheduled for the next strategic planning cycle.
My uncle knows which way north is. His truck has never asked him to accept terms and conditions.
The government launched an app to help you save. It requires a new phone.
My town has a printer that predates the internet. It has never asked for a subscription.
Dad doesn’t believe in throwing money at a problem. He believes in shining a flashlight at it while I get the right wrench.
They scheduled a town meeting on public participation. At two in the afternoon. On a Tuesday.
Mom bought a dented can for half price. She said the green beans didn’t know.
Congress debated a cap on borrowing. In the end it agreed to call it a roof with expansion potential.
When does a small town become a big city? When the barber needs your last name.
I asked Grandpa about his passive income. He said the hens were reasonably active.
The parks department asked how long a bench should last. An old bench in the park declined to speculate.
Our family believes in checks and balances. Dad writes the check. Mom checks the balance.
The grant is designed to help very small businesses. You need a full-time employee to apply for it.
The town finally got a suggestion box. Its first suggestion was a less expensive suggestion box.
Grandma’s recipe says “feeds eight.” Her foreign policy is feeding twelve.
Washington says the spending bill is historic. Judging by the interest, so will my grandchildren.
